text: Thus he lived for many years, with short periods of rest, honored by the world, yet he was mostly in a gloomy mood, which only deepened because no one took it seriously. <break time="0.8s" /> When some kind hearted person suggested that his sadness probably came from hunger, the artist might reply, especially late in a fast, with a burst of fury, shaking the bars of his cage like an animal. <break time="0.8s" /> The impresario had a way of handling such outbursts, for he would apologize to the audience on the artists behalf, admitting that only the irritability caused by fasting, which well fed people could hardly understand, could excuse such behavior. <break time="0.8s" /> He would then praise the artists claim that he could fast far longer than forty days, while at the same time showing photographs of him on the fortieth day, lying in bed almost dead from exhaustion. <break time="0.8s" /> This twisting of the truth was more than he could bear, for his exhaustion, really the result of being stopped too early, was presented here as the very reason for stopping him. <break time="0.8s" /> To fight against this misunderstanding, against an entire world that refused to understand, was impossible, so each time he would sink back onto the straw with a sigh, and the reassured public could approach the cage once more. <break time="0.8s" /> A few years later, however, a sudden change took place, for the public that had once crowded to see him turned away from fasting displays to other amusements, and the impresarios tour through Europe met with indifference everywhere. <break time="0.8s" /> Too old to change his profession and too devoted to fasting to give it up, the hunger artist parted from the impresario and hired himself out to a large circus, where his cage was placed near the animal stables.
